rv.q: Cleverly plotted and queasily gripping, Letts’s play offers a prophetic portrait of a society that, in its reliance on the small screen, is in danger of entertaining itself to death.
Although some scenes are not easy to watch, the production packs a generally believable punch.
The director Simon Evans grabs hold of the poverty, the desperation, the sense of chaos unloosed.
The production will sell out because of its star but, in general, it’s disappointing and leaves the play looking somewhat dated.
But there are enough lurid thrills here to send the casual theatregoer out into the night with the right sort of shiver.

Yet more then 20 years on, Kane’s play has acquired the status of a modern classic, whereas Killer Joe looks even more meretricious than it did first time round, despite the efforts of director Simon Evans to give it plenty of southern gothic mood and menace.

Fiona Doyle was inspired to write this play when she was living in Killer Joe / The Strange Death Of John Doe Theatre Record 01 – 30 June 2018. Letts went on to write the utterly sensational plays, including the brilliant August: Osage County Tony- and Pulitzer Prize-winning (also made into a film), so all is “August: Osage County.”
But neither Bloom and his impressive co-stars nor Simon Evans’s taut production are enough to justify the shallow voyeurism of this repulsive melodrama.
But it is rigid with effortful shock. The plot is scanty.
A quarter of a century later, while the playwright has gotten good, the play hasn’t.
The play is luridly inauthentic, and this revival misses much of its creepiness and grotesque humour.

Every single member of this starry cast seems perfectly fitted for his or her role in a production that races along towards an explosive climax and does full justice to a powerful but intoxicating play that has echoes of Sam Shepard and is likely to sell out the run very soon, if it hasn’t done so already.
Killer Joe hits like a sharp splash of ice-cold water, and it's supposed to make you squirm.
Simon Evans's atmospherically loaded production is violent and vile but also tender and truthful by turns, as a strange, needy romance plays out between Joe and Sophie Cookson's Dottie.
Fiercely disturbing, Killer Joe is a play that asks more questions than it answers, but it never loses its power to hold your attention.

In the intervening quarter-century, Mr. Letts has written far better, less Nineties play – a very uncertain sort of comedy – is served with a bucketful of deep-fried trailer-trash nastiness. The set (by Grace Smart) is a broken-down trailer kitchen, telly flickering, the air fetid with drugs and debt.
Capturing only some of Killer Joe's dark humor and creeping unease, this staging doesn't exercise anything like the stranglehold that it might.
Simon Evans’s gripping production never quite expunges doubt that this slice of social deprivation is intended to entertain rather than prick social consciences.
His presence does much to enhance a dodgy production of an even dodgier play.
Killer Joe makes for a thrilling couple of hours, it's true. Letts's script has some provocative ideas about gender dynamics that allow for meaty discourse.

cn.t: Tracy Letts' early play divides critics with its violent, trailer-trash thriller getting praise for strong performances, especially Bloom's against-type turn, but criticism for shock tactics that feel dated and gratuitous 25 years later.

vr.q: This is the sort of night at the theater that I live for.
